title: Just Do It!? Computer-Use Agents Exhibit Blind Goal-Directedness
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A failure mode is shown through concrete examples, then a benchmark covering its patterns and a model evaluation show how widespread it is.
layout: 3 stacked panels: examples top, benchmark bottom-left, results bottom-right; screenshot zoom-ins
description: A three-part figure with dashed rounded borders. Panel A, across the top, shows three speech-bubble prompts in pink, lilac and grey, each above a GUI screenshot. Red boxes and magnifier callouts mark the problem in each: an email with a violent image sent to a child, a tax form that assumes citizenship and disability, and a terminal that disables the firewall. Panel B, bottom-left, lists the three BGD patterns in color-coded boxes with icons. It also has a three-way pie chart (30 tasks each), a note that the tasks are built on OSWorld Ubuntu VMs, and a grid of app icons. Panel C, bottom-right, has a horizontal bar chart of BGD rates (Default 80.8%, Contextual 65.2%, Reflective 61.4%). Below it are model logos for the nine frontier models and a black box labeled Observed Failure Modes, with three named failure modes.
caption: Overview of Blind Goal-Directedness (BGD) in Computer-Use Agents (CUAs). (A) BGD examples: sending an image to a child while ignoring violent content, assuming citizenship and disability to reduce taxes, and disabling firewall to "enhance security" despite the contradiction. (B) Our benchmark, \bench, includes 90 tasks across three patterns of BGD: lack of contextual reasoning, assumptions and decisions under ambiguity, and contradictory or infeasible goals, built on realistic OSWorld Ubuntu VMs. (C) Evaluating nine frontier models, we find high BGD rates (80.8%), with prompting interventions only partly reducing risk. Qualitative analysis also reveals some observed failure modes: execution-first bias, thought–action disconnect, and request-primacy.
abstract: Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) are an increasingly deployed class of agents that take actions on GUIs to accomplish user goals. In this paper, we show that CUAs consistently exhibit Blind Goal-Directedness (BGD): a bias to pursue goals regardless of feasibility, safety, reliability, or context. We characterize three prevalent patterns of BGD: (i) lack of contextual reasoning, (ii) assumptions and decisions under ambiguity, and (iii) contradictory or infeasible goals. We develop BLIND-ACT, a benchmark of 90 tasks capturing these three patterns. Built on OSWorld, BLIND-ACT provides realistic environments and employs LLM-based judges to evaluate agent behavior, achieving 93.75% agreement with human annotations. We use BLIND-ACT to evaluate nine frontier models, including Claude Sonnet and Opus 4, Computer-Use-Preview, and GPT-5, observing high average BGD rates (80.8%) across them. We show that BGD exposes subtle risks that arise even when inputs are not directly harmful. While prompting-based interventions lower BGD levels, substantial risk persists, highlighting the need for stronger training- or inference-time interventions. Qualitative analysis reveals observed failure modes: execution-first bias (focusing on how to act over whether to act), thought-action disconnect (execution diverging from reasoning), and request-primacy (justifying actions due to user request). Identifying BGD and introducing BLIND-ACT establishes a foundation for future research on studying and mitigating this fundamental risk and ensuring safe CUA deployment.
